prompt:
Write an essay of about 800 words on the subject below.

Write it the way an excellent, idiosyncratic human essayist would: someone with real expertise and strong opinions, writing in the first person for their own blog. Commit to a specific thesis that a thoughtful reader might disagree with. Use concrete particulars (names, numbers, incidents, things only someone who had done the work would know) in place of general statements. Vary sentence length. No headings, no bullet points, no summary paragraph at the end, and none of the stock phrases of AI writing.

Output only the essay, with no title.

Subject: an essay about the Erie Canal and what it changed
raw:
The Erie Canal should have failed. I want to say that up front, because everything worth knowing about the canal follows from the fact that it was an absurd project undertaken by absurd people in an absurd place, and it worked anyway. When Dewitt Clinton first pushed the scheme in 1817, the New York legislature had to be shamed into it—the measure passed by a razor margin only after Clinton allies traded votes on a banking bill—and the federal government wanted nothing to do with it. Jefferson, when Clinton sounding him out years earlier, told him the thing was "a little short of madness." Madison vetoed a national internal improvements bill in 1817 on constitutional grounds. So New York went alone, borrowing $7 million—more than a quarter of the entire federal budget that year—on the credit of a state with maybe a million people in it.

And the engineers were worse than the finances. There was, essentially, no one in the United States who had ever built a canal of consequence. Benjamin Wright, who ran the middle section, was a judge from Rome, New York, who had surveyed turnpike(roads). Canvass White was a 25-year-old who went to England at his own expense, walked existing canals, took notes, came back, and invented a waterproof cement—hydrolic limestone, hydrate of lime, they called it Roman cement—because American mortar kept washing out. The locks were timber at first, later stone, 90 feet by 15, dimensioned to a boat that existed only on paper. They dug through 363 miles of what was mostly wilderness, much of it malarial swamp west of Syracuse, where workers died of "canal fever" at rates the state preferred not to publish. The Irish did the rock cuts near Lockport, which took two years of blasting through that Niagara escarpment and killed an unknown number of them. The Champlain canal was premature; the Chemung and Oswego branches came late; the whole thing was, in the words of one 1820s critic, "the prince of jobs."

It opened in October 1825, and Clinton poured a keg of Lake Erie water into the Atlantic at Sandy Hook in a ceremony called the Wedding of the Waters, which is exactly the kind of self-congratulating pageant you'd expect from the canal's chief salesman. Fine. Mock it. But look at what happened to the numbers. Freight from Buffalo to New York City, which had cost roughly $100 a ton and taken weeks by wagon and coastwise ship, dropped to under $10 a ton within a couple of years and kept falling. The trip went from roughly three weeks to eight days. Passenger packets made Buffalo to Albany in three and a half at a walking pace plus lock time, and people wrote home about it the way you'd write about a new subway. In 1820 maybe 3,000 people a year entered what's now western New York by the canal route; within a decade the state's western population more than tripled. Rochester went from a village of a few hundred when digging started to a city of 10,000 by 1830, its mills grinding flour because the canal ran right through them at a 26-foot drop—the waterfalls that had been scenery became hydropower and the canal became the shipment. Buffalo, a town of 2,000 in 1820, was the world's largest grain port for a stretch of the 1840s. Syracuse existed, essentially, because there was salt at Onondaga and the canal could carry it; "salt spray" was the mud around the brine vats.

Here is my actual thesis, and it's not the one the plaques give you. The canal is usually taught as a transportation story: cheaper freight, eastern markets for western grain. That's true but it's the least interesting part. What actually changed was the geography of ambition and capital. Before 1825, the American interior was a colonial economy of whatever Europe. New Orleans was the outlet of the whole Mississippi basin, and exports went to Europe, and the interior's wealth was priced in Liverpool. After 1825, the interior and the Atlantic seaboard became one market, and then one country in a way the constitution alone had never managed. New York City became the entrepôt not because its harbor was better than Philadelphia's or Boston's—this is a myth the city tells itself—but because it sat at the seaward end of the cheap interior. The commission merchants, the packet lines, the insurance pool, the wharves: all of that followed the canal, then compounded after the railroads came, which themselves were started with canal profits and canal expertise. And it wasn't only commerce. The canal carried the evangelical networks: Charles Finney's revivalism moved west along it, and so did the reform movements that came out of the burned-over district of western New York—the same stretch of canal-fed boom towns that produced Mormonism at Palmyra, the Fox sisters at Hydesville, and the Seneca Falls convention in 1848. When people say "radical ideas flourish in boomtowns," the Erie Canal corridor is the evidence.

What it destroyed matters too, and I think this is where the popular picture is weakest. The canal killed New Orleans's claim to the entire trans-Appalachian funnel; Philadelphia and Baltimore were so alarmed they chartered competing works, including the Baltimore & Ohio railroad, which is to say the canal's greatest influence was producing its own successor technology through competition. And the canal region broke treaties. The toll revenue that paid off the entire $7 million debt by 1834 (yes, paid off, eight years early) rested in part on a transportation system that ran through lands of the Haudenosaunee that had persuaded them a decade earlier to cede; the canal lobby's land speculation fed the anti-transport campaigns in the legislature, campaigns that the canal itself made wealthier and more numerous. And when the railroads came through in the 1840s and 50s, the same corridor that had boomed was left a string of towns whose growth flatlined. Syracuse recovered; the villages between it and Newark, the ones whose grain went to Rochester mills instead, didn't.

So I'd revise the madness comment. Jefferson was right on the engineering and wrong about everything else. The canal worked not because it was beautiful but because the state was the only player big enough and patient enough to do it, and because the returns were not in tolls but in the value created all around it—land, cities, industry, taxes. That is a lesson we keep relearning badly. Every decade or so someone proposes "another Erie Canal"—some giant infrastructure plan sold on direct returns—and it flops, because the actual canal's payoff was diffuse, social and speculative all at once. If you want to understand why Upstate New York feels simultaneously grand and depleted, drive route 31 along the old alignment. You'll pass the widened 1905 barge canal beside towns full of second-empire storefronts pitched at heeltapping lock foundations, a monument to the fact that infrastructure moves history once and then sits there while history goes on without it.
